doc.title: Carmen Caramanica interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, July 27, 2011

title: First charts for The Tonight Show and a solo with the band
summary: He wrote two charts for Rawls's Tonight Show spot, heard them played perfectly, and was given a solo by Doc Severinsen.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: But I did watch how Reg conducted the band and talked to him about how he wrote things, and he was also a wonderful mentor to me. He exposed me to stuff that I’d never thought of. So he said “look, just take the gig. If it doesn’t work out for you then you can go back to being the guitar player. They’re not going to fire you, and they’ll get another musical director or arranger.” Okay fine. So I did it. And the first assignment I got was well we’re going to do “The Tonight Show.” And we need two charts that we don’t have, for Lou to sing on this thing. And so here’s Shelly Cohen’s number. Shelly Cohen was the musical director for “The Tonight Show.” Doc Severinsen was the conductor and Tommy Newsome was the second director. But when you dealt with the Tonight Show Band you dealt with Shelly Cohen, who did everything from music clearance to telling you what you need, and so we had a situation where we were going to do something that called for strings and he said “well the budget for this particular act doesn’t call for strings so can you do it for flutes instead?” So he would have this whole system that he would work out, the whole politics of it. So that was my first time I had to do something, and actually score it for a professional band. I’d done some smaller bands around here, but this was like oh boy. So I brought my little keyboard into the hotel rooms, and I sweated blood over every note until I finally got everything to be “I think this worked. Let me try this again. Let me play this again.”
Because there was no — this was like way pre-Finale days where you could hear it back.

Oh absolutely. You could not hear a thing. You had to go “let’s see, here’s how I voiced the brass, okay that’s right.” Of course I can’t play keyboard worth anything anyway so everything was for slow motion. Now the saxes under that, yeah that should work. Now do I really want? No don’t do that. This kind of thing. So I somehow got through writing these things to the point where I thought I think they’re going to work and of course I was very familiar with the style because by this time I’d been playing with Lou and I knew the kind of stuff he liked to hear, I knew his history. So in any event, we got to the rehearsal and all I had to do was go one-two-three-four, and this wonderful band kicked in and it was like — bong — this sounded so cool. It was like amazing. You know everything worked. And when you have wonderful musicians that do this every day, it’s magic. And it makes you look really good.
And you’re kind of standing there like “yeah I knew this was going to work.”

I don’t know, I think there was a little puddle of sweat by the time we did both songs. But it really came out nice. And then as kind of another little pat on the back, Doc Severinsen was on this particular show, and a lot of times he wasn’t there and Tommy was there. But he said “when we do the break, let’s give the guitar player some. So there was this, I don’t know, some blues thing or something like that. And so they got to that section, and we’ll be back in a few minutes. And so he points to me and I’m soloing with the Tonight © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -8-
Show Band. For about ten seconds you heard it and then it faded out for a dog food commercial or something like that.
And this was on the west coast?
This was on the west coast, right.
After they moved. Wow that’s a thrill.
